content: The occurrence of side effects attributable to ethionamide in children under or over 2 years of age has not been well-documented. The only available evidence pertains to children, with no data available for adults. The anticipated desirable effects of ethionamide treatment are uncertain. The implementation of preventive treatment for contacts of MDR-TB cases requires access to drug-susceptibility testing for the index case. This ensures that the preventive treatment regimen for the contact can be tailored to the resistance profile of the index case. Additionally, close and careful monitoring of adverse events is necessary. An alternative approach, such as close clinical monitoring, also demands resources, primarily in the form of healthcare staff. The summary of judgments indicates varying levels of support for follow-up versus tailored treatment. The expert panel suggests against treatment over follow-up, does not recommend tailored treatment, and suggests either tailored treatment or follow-up as options. However, they recommend tailored treatment in certain cases. The panel concluded that the evidence was inadequate to make definitive recommendations. There is an urgent need for further research on the benefits and risks of preventive therapy in contacts of MDR-TB cases. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are particularly needed to determine the optimal drugs, dosages, and durations for preventive therapy. In children in contact with MDR-TB cases, the evidence for prophylaxis versus no prophylaxis is very low. Children who received preventive therapy were at higher risk for developing TB due to factors such as younger age, higher rates of infection, more sputum smear-positive index cases, and less frequent prior treatment or preventive therapy. No adjustments were made for confounding factors. The GRADE system defines the certainty of evidence as follows: High: The research provides a very good indication of the likely effect, with a low likelihood of substantial differences. Moderate: The research provides a good indication of the likely effect, with a moderate likelihood of substantial differences. Low: The research provides some indication of the likely effect, but the likelihood of substantial differences is high. Very Low: The research does not provide a reliable indication of the likely effect, and the likelihood of substantial differences is very high. The GRADE Working Group, established in 2000, developed a common, sensible, and transparent approach to grading the quality of evidence and the strength of recommendations. This approach addresses the shortcomings of previous grading systems in healthcare. Many international organizations have contributed to its development and have adopted its use.
